summary: Codex has a deliberately layered, privacy-conscious observability stack centered on the Rust tracing ecosystem bridged into OpenTelemetry by a dedicated codex-otel crate. Roughly 2,000 log call sites (warn! dominant), 81 #[instrument] spans and ~190 metric call sites feed per-binary subscriber stacks: an opt-in 0600 file log and a local SQLite log database for the TUI, stderr for exec and app-server, an in-memory feedback ring buffer, and OTLP log/trace/metric exporters. Defaults are conservative and asymmetric: log and trace export are off unless configured, while the metrics exporter defaults to Statsig - an OTLP-HTTP push to ab.chatgpt.com with an embedded client key - in release builds when analytics is enabled (the TUI passes default_analytics_enabled=true). User prompts are redacted by default ([REDACTED] unless otel.log_user_prompt=true), metric tags are sanitized and low-cardinality, and a curated disable-list keeps token-usage/API metrics off the built-in Statsig route. Crash reporting is consent-based: no sentry::init anywhere; panic hooks restore the terminal and log via tracing, and Sentry envelopes are only uploaded when the user explicitly submits feedback (with a 4 MiB in-memory log ring attached). codex doctor provides a redacted, read-mostly diagnostic report. The main gaps: a local operator sees almost nothing by default (metrics go to OpenAI, not to the user; file logging is opt-in; exec filters at error), the TypeScript/Python SDKs emit no telemetry of their own, and rollout flush errors are discarded at session-seed call sites (mitigated by recorder-internal warn+retry).

findings.title: Structured tracing logging (~2,000 call sites) with per-binary sinks; file logging is opt-in and 0600
findings.description: All Rust crates log through the tracing ecosystem (~1,995 macro call sites; warn! dominates at 1,175 vs 253 error!, a deliberate 'observable but non-fatal' style). Each binary assembles its own subscriber stack: the TUI writes a file log only when log_dir is explicitly configured in config.toml (created append-only with mode 0600, default filter codex_core=info,codex_tui=info,codex_rmcp_client=info, overridable via RUST_LOG); codex exec logs to stderr with a default filter of 'error' (OTel SDK noise explicitly silenced); the app-server logs to stderr honoring RUST_LOG with an optional LOG_FORMAT=json mode. So log destinations and verbosity are consistent in mechanism but intentionally different per surface.

findings.title: Logs are additionally persisted to a local SQLite 'logs' database at TRACE level
findings.description: Both the TUI and app-server attach a log_db layer that ships tracing events through a bounded queue into a dedicated 'logs' SQLite database in the state store. Its default filter is TRACE with noisy targets (hyper_util, sqlx internals) capped or off, and the OTel export targets (codex_otel.log_only / codex_otel.trace_safe) explicitly excluded so exported telemetry events are not double-written locally. This gives post-hoc local debuggability even when no file log is configured.

findings.title: User prompts are redacted by default; exported log events carry account id/email, trace events do not
findings.description: Telemetry events are emitted through two tracing targets: codex_otel.log_only and codex_otel.trace_safe. The log_event! macro attaches user.account_id and user.email to every event, while the trace_safe variant omits them - a deliberate two-tier privacy split between the log export path and the span/trace path. Prompt content is redacted by default: otel.log_user_prompt defaults to false, in which case the codex.user_prompt event logs the literal string [REDACTED] plus only the prompt length; the trace event never carries the prompt at all. These identity fields only leave the machine if a log exporter is configured (off by default, see telemetry-pipeline).

findings.title: Centralized metric catalog (~60 named counters/histograms) covering turns, tools, API, transport and startup
findings.description: All metric names live in one names.rs module (~60 constants under the codex.* prefix): tool call counts/durations, API request counts/durations, SSE/WebSocket event timings, turn end-to-end/TTFT/token-usage, guardian reviews, goals, plugins, hooks, and startup phases. About 190 call sites outside the otel crate emit through a shared best-effort metrics client (errors returned, never panicking the caller). Cardinality is actively managed: tag values pass sanitize_metric_tag_value (charset-restricted, 256-char cap) and comments mark tags as low-cardinality by design, so the catalog is safe to aggregate downstream.

findings.title: Panic hooks restore the terminal and forward panics to tracing without swallowing default reports
findings.description: The TUI installs chained panic hooks: one restores the terminal and re-emits the panic through tracing::error! before delegating to the previous (color-eyre) hook so users still get a full backtrace, and a second in tui.rs restores the terminal on panic while explicitly ignoring restore errors. Telemetry initialization itself is wrapped in catch_unwind in both the TUI and exec entry points, so a panicking OTel provider degrades to 'no telemetry' instead of crashing the app - the observer cannot take down the observed.

findings.title: Sentry is used only for user-initiated feedback envelopes; no automatic crash reporting
findings.description: There is no sentry::init call anywhere in the workspace - the Sentry SDK is used purely as an envelope builder/uploader inside the feedback crate. A tracing layer keeps the last ~4 MiB of filtered logs in an in-memory ring buffer; only when the user explicitly submits feedback (TUI /feedback flow or the app-server feedback request) is an envelope with those logs and diagnostic attachments (doctor report, sandbox logs, tool caches) uploaded to a hardcoded Sentry DSN. Crashes are therefore visible to operators only if users report them - a consent-first posture that trades fleet-wide crash visibility for privacy.

findings.title: Rollout flush errors are discarded at session-seed call sites
findings.description: In the session bootstrap path (seeding new and forked threads), flush_rollout() returns an io::Result that is discarded with let _ = at both call sites, so a failed flush of the conversation rollout - the persistence layer resume/fork depends on - produces no signal at that decision point. The blast radius is limited because the rollout recorder itself warns and retries internally when the writer fails ('failed to {operation} rollout writer; reopening and retrying'), and persistence metrics exist; but the caller cannot distinguish 'flushed' from 'silently failed', which matters on the path that decides whether a thread is durably file-backed.

findings.title: codex doctor provides a redacted, read-mostly diagnostic report wired into support flows
findings.description: The CLI ships a dedicated doctor subcommand that inspects installation, configuration, authentication, terminal, state paths and bounded reachability probes without mutating state or starting services; each check returns a redacted serializable row backing both the human summary and --json output. It is integrated into the support loop: the redacted doctor JSON is a named attachment on feedback uploads, and state-database recovery errors direct users to run it. There are no long-running health/readiness endpoints - appropriate for a local CLI whose 'health surface' is a diagnostic command rather than a probe URL.

findings.title: Metrics default to a Statsig exporter: OTLP-HTTP to ab.chatgpt.com with an embedded client key, release builds only
findings.description: While log and trace exporters default to None, otel.metrics_exporter defaults to Statsig, which resolves to an OTLP-HTTP/JSON push to https://ab.chatgpt.com/otlp/v1/metrics authenticated with a client API key embedded in the source. The default is disabled in debug builds and gated at runtime on analytics_enabled (the TUI passes default_analytics_enabled=true), so a stock release install with analytics on sends usage/performance metrics to OpenAI by default. Mitigations are real: only sanitized low-cardinality metric data is sent (no prompts or log content), and a curated STATSIG_DISABLED_METRICS list keeps token-usage, API-call and tool-call metrics off the built-in route while still delivering them to any user-configured OTLP exporter. Worth flagging because 'metrics on by default to the vendor' is a posture users and enterprises will want to know about and how to opt out of (analytics_enabled=false or metrics_exporter='none').

evidence.note: asymmetric defaults: traces off, metrics -> Statsig
hardcoded endpoint and client key (debug builds resolve to None at lines 20-21)
token-usage/API metrics excluded from the built-in Statsig route

findings.recommendation: Document the default metrics destination and the opt-outs (analytics_enabled = false, otel.metrics_exporter = "none") prominently in user-facing docs, and treat the embedded Statsig client key as rotatable configuration rather than source-embedded.

findings.title: Per-signal OTLP export (HTTP/gRPC, headers, mutual TLS) with batching and a bounded shutdown flush
findings.description: The codex-otel crate exposes independent exporter settings per signal (logs, traces, metrics), each accepting OtlpHttp (JSON or binary protobuf) or OtlpGrpc with custom headers and optional mutual TLS (CA, client cert/key). Standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*_TIMEOUT environment variables are honored, spans go through batch processors, and shutdown is handled by a detached worker with an explicit time budget so a hung collector cannot block process exit ('telemetry shutdown exceeded its time budget'). This means any enterprise can point Codex at its own collector and get logs, spans and the full metric catalog without code changes.

findings.title: Separate product-analytics event pipeline posts to the ChatGPT backend with a bounded, lossy queue
findings.description: Alongside OTel metrics, a codex-analytics crate batches structured product events (guardian reviews, compaction, goals, tool calls, invocation facts) through a reducer and posts them to {base_url}/codex/analytics-events/events on the authenticated ChatGPT backend. The channel is bounded and deliberately lossy - when the queue is full it drops events and emits tracing::warn!("dropping analytics events: queue is full") - so analytics backpressure cannot stall the agent. A debug-build capture-file mode exists for inspecting what would be sent. This is a second, product-focused egress path distinct from the Statsig metrics route, gated by the same analytics enablement.

findings.title: With an OTLP collector configured, the emitted signals support rich fleet dashboards and alerting
findings.description: An operator who points otel.exporter/trace_exporter/metrics_exporter at their own collector can build substantial monitoring from what the code already emits: alerting on model API error rates and latency (codex.api_request + duration histograms), turn health (e2e/TTFT/token-usage histograms), tool-call failure rates and durations, SSE/WebSocket transport stalls, startup-phase regressions, guardian review outcomes, and SQLite persistence errors (rollout/DB telemetry recorders). Session-lifecycle log events (with per-conversation ids, model, auth mode) enable per-session forensic timelines, and W3C trace propagation lets Codex spans join a larger distributed trace. OpenAI itself, via the default Statsig route, sees a narrower slice: process starts, turns, goals, startup timings - with API/token/tool metrics deliberately excluded from that route.

findings.title: Blind spots: a default install is nearly dark locally, and the SDK/JS surfaces emit nothing
findings.description: Several failure modes are invisible today. (1) A default install gives the local user almost no signals: file logging requires configuring log_dir, exec's stderr filter is 'error', and the metrics that do flow by default go to OpenAI's Statsig endpoint - not anywhere the user can see - so 'why is my Codex slow/failing' is answerable only via opt-in logs, the SQLite log db, or codex doctor. (2) Crash visibility is consent-bound: with no automatic crash reporter, panics that users do not report leave no operator-side trace. (3) The TypeScript SDK sources contain no logging or telemetry calls at all, and the thin npm/python wrappers likewise emit nothing, so integrations built on the SDKs are dark unless the spawned Rust binary's telemetry is configured. (4) Anything OpenAI might want to alert on fleet-wide beyond the curated Statsig metric slice (e.g. API error rates, which are on the disabled list) is structurally unavailable from the default pipeline.

evidence.note: file logging exists only when explicitly configured
log export off by default; the SDK dark spots are absences and cannot be cited
